parts: Raja, the narrator, is an innocent, adventurous young boy who likes to meddle with creatures like snakes and bees. His grandparents care deeply about his safety. The story shows how a small misunderstanding grows because Raja is not allowed to speak, and how people put blind faith in untrained 'medicine men'.

One day Raja sees a small snake in the compound. When it sees him, it hides in a coconut shell. Raja closes the mouth of the shell with a stone and proudly runs to Grandmother: 'Look, Grandma, I have caught a snake.' Grandmother is shocked and cries for help. Grandfather snatches the shell and throws it away; the snake crawls into the bushes. He warns Raja never to go near a snake, because snakes are very dangerous.

In the evening Raja tries to catch a bee and it stings his finger. He runs to Grandmother saying he has been 'bitten'. She thinks a snake has bitten him and calls Grandfather. Seeing a blue mark on the finger, Grandfather, without a word, picks Raja up and runs across the garden and paddy fields to the house of an old grey-haired man who is believed to cure snake bite.

The old man makes Raja sit still, takes water in a small brass vessel and recites mantras. Raja wants to say that it was a bee, not a snake, but Grandfather holds him tight and does not let him talk. Grandmother and other people arrive and watch sadly and silently. By now the pain has stopped, but Raja still has to sit and be 'cured'. Finally the old man washes the finger, gives Raja water to drink and announces, 'Thank God, you brought Raja in time. He is out of danger now. It was indeed a poisonous snake that bit him.' Everyone thanks him for the 'magic cure', and Grandfather sends him gifts.

(1) Timely and effective communication is important — silence is not always good; if Raja had been allowed to speak, the confusion would have been avoided. (2) We should think critically about superstitions and blind faith in untrained medicine men; in an emergency we should get proper medical help. (3) Not all snakes are dangerous; animals act out of fear and should not be teased. (4) The grandparents' love and concern for Raja is touching, even though their reaction is based on a misunderstanding.

Raja — the narrator, an innocent, curious boy. Grandmother — loving and easily alarmed; thinks the bee sting is a snake bite. Grandfather — caring and quick to act; carries Raja to the medicine man but does not let him speak. The old grey-haired man — the 'medicine man' who recites mantras and claims to have cured a snake bite.
